S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor occurring within three months of the onset of that stressor. The reaction is clinically significant, marked by distress that is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, but does not meet criteria for another specific mental disorder. Symptoms typically resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though it can become persistent if the stressor is ongoing. It is differentiated from normal stress reactions by the degree of impairment and disproportionate response, and from disorders like major depressive disorder or PTSD by its timing, milder and more situational nature, and the absence of a characteristic symptom cluster.

patient.personality: Timothy is a structured, competitive, and analytical coach who prides himself on meticulous planning, community mentorship, and keeping tight control over his environment.
patient.stressor: Timothy’s difficulties began when his college athletics program hired a new athletic director who abruptly changed priorities, cutting funding for his team and imposing a results-at-all-costs culture that clashed with his data-driven, developmental approach. Over a few weeks, he found long-standing routines disrupted: practice times were shifted with little notice, key support staff were let go, and he was pressured to bench athletes he’d been carefully mentoring in favor of short-term wins. As someone who depends heavily on structure and sees his role as both coach and protector of his players, he felt increasingly trapped between his values and the new demands, and he began bringing more work home, arguing with his spouse about late nights, and withdrawing from his usual hobbies like home brewing and pickup basketball. After about a month of escalating strain at work and growing tension at home that started to interfere with his ability to focus during practices and outreach events, his wife and a fellow coach urged him to talk to a mental health professional about how overwhelmed and unlike himself he had become.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since all the changes at work, I feel like I’m not handling the stress well at all and it’s starting to affect everything I do.”

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.
S081.manifestation: Since all the changes with the new director, I’ve been way more on edge and not myself—I’ll snap at my players over small mistakes, feel this tight knot in my chest before practice, then go home and just sit there staring at my laptop reworking practice plans instead of enjoying time with my wife or doing anything I usually like.
